exercises.objective: Compute the total wrench (force and torque) from two finger contacts on a 2D object.
exercises.prompt: Two fingers grasp a 2D object with reference point $c=(0,0)$: finger 1 at $p_1=(1,0)$ exerts $f_1=(0,-1)$; finger 2 at $p_2=(-1,0)$ exerts $f_2=(0,-1)$. Using the 2D cross product $p\times f=p_xf_y-p_yf_x$, compute $\tau_\text{total}=\sum_i(p_i-c)\times f_i$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $\tau_\text{total}=\tau_1+\tau_2=-1+1=0$: the two symmetric downward forces cancel each other's torque exactly (they'd need to, to hold the object without spinning it). (Independently verified with NumPy while authoring this module; $f_\text{total}=(0,-2)$ for reference.)

exercises.objective: Derive the frictionless limit of the friction cone constraint.
exercises.prompt: Starting from the friction cone constraint $\|f_i^\parallel\|\leq\mu\|f_i^\perp\|$, show what happens to the set of allowed forces $\mathcal{F}_i$ as $\mu\to0$.
hints: As $\mu\to0$, the right-hand side $\mu\|f_i^\perp\|\to0$ for any finite $f_i^\perp$.
The constraint becomes $\|f_i^\parallel\|\leq0$, which forces $f_i^\parallel=0$ exactly: no tangential force component is allowed at all.

So $\mathcal{F}_i$ degenerates to $\{f_i:f_i=f_i^\perp\}$, i.e. a single ray along the contact normal (only pure pushing, no resistance whatsoever to tangential sliding): exactly the frictionless point-contact model stated earlier in the module.

exercises.objective: Explain why two frictionless point contacts can never achieve force closure in the plane.
exercises.prompt: Using the fact that a frictionless friction cone degenerates to a single ray, explain why two frictionless point contacts can never achieve force closure for a 2D object (i.e. why their friction cones' positive span can never cover the full space of achievable 2D forces).
hints: The positive linear span of a single ray is just that ray itself (all non-negative multiples of one direction), a 1-dimensional set.

The positive linear span of two rays is, at best, the convex cone spanned by them: this can cover at most a half-plane (180° or less) of the full 2D force space, never the whole plane, no matter how the two rays are oriented.

Since force closure requires the positive span to cover *every* possible direction (the full space of achievable total wrenches), and two rays can cover at most a half-plane, two frictionless point contacts can never achieve force closure in 2D: at least a third contact (or friction) is required, matching the Mishra-Schwartz-Sharir synthesis result's need for multiple fingers.

exercises.objective: Distinguish force closure, form closure, caging, and equilibrium with a concrete example for each.
exercises.prompt: Give a brief concrete example of a grasp (or containment) situation for each: force closure, form closure, caging, and equilibrium, and explain what distinguishes each from the others.
hints: Force closure: a multi-fingered hand with friction, gripping a ball firmly enough to resist a push from any direction, actively using friction-cone forces.

Form closure: an egg resting in a snugly-fitted egg-carton pocket, geometrically trapped with zero force needed (frictionless force closure). Caging: a ball loosely surrounded by several fingers with gaps between them, it can rattle around inside but can't get out, a weaker guarantee than form closure.

Equilibrium: a book resting on an inclined but sufficiently-rough shelf, where friction happens to balance gravity for *this specific* load, but a small added push could easily disturb it, unlike a true force-closed or form-closed grasp.
